feed.title: MetaLichen Lab
feed.subtitle: Our work focuses on fungal-algal symbioses, known as lichens. How is it possible that multiple microbes - fungi, algae, bacteria - self-assemble into a lichen, which is big, complex, and three-dimensional? How can symbiotic interactions lead to a stable body plan? How do lichen architectures develop and grow? To address these questions, we use meta-omics, microscopy, and cell biology tools. Our ultimate goal is to study lichen symbiosis as a case of complexity arising in evolution. The lab opens in April 2026, stay tuned for updates!

entry.title: Tangerine, a Starship element in the genome of Xanthoria is a representative of a new Starship family unique to lichens

link.title: Tangerine, a Starship element in the genome of Xanthoria is a representative of a new Starship family unique to lichens

entry.content:
Our paper on Tangerine the lichen Starship is out in PNAS! See below the summary of this study 👇

Discovery of giant transposons Starships challenged what we thought we knew about fungal genomes. But what about Starships in lichen fungi? In the paper, we present the Tangerine element from Xanthoria parietina. Tangerine has all hallmark features of a Starship: 100 kb in length, the captain gene responsible for transposition, as well as accessory genes and ‘cargo’.

Tangerine’s captain didn’t fit into any existing family of Starship captains, but in the tree it grouped together with several genes from other lichen fungi. After expanding our analyses to many more genomes, we were able to describe the clade as the new family, the Tangerine-family, unique to Lecanoromycetes.

Coolest part for me is the tantalizing possibility that Tangerine might have mediated horizontal gene transfer (HGT) between different fungi present within a lichen thallus. Two genes from Tangerine appear to have been horizontally transferred from Chaetothyriales, a group of black fungi. Some Chaetothyriales are stably associated with certain lichens, and our earlier evidence suggest that they can be present in Xanthoria as well. We found other potential HGT events linked to Starships too by juxtaposing phylogenetic tree of the captains with the species phylogeny.

Our little Tangerine is undoubtedly not the only Starship present in lichens! Hopefully we will soon know more about their diversity and what kind of role they play in the evolution of lichen fungi.

entry.title: International Association for Lichenology congress in Trieste

link.title: International Association for Lichenology congress in Trieste

entry.content:
The International Association for Lichenology congress happened in Trieste in the last week of July. It has been 10 years since the last in-person IAL! Gulnara has presented her posdoc research on Xanthoria omics and secreted proteins as a keynote talk on the final day of the conference.

It was an incredible conference! Great to meet so many new people and re-connect with old friends!

entry.title: Aino Henssen Award
entry.content: During the IAL congress Gulnara recieved the Aino Henssen Award for outstanding postdoctoral research on lichen symbiosis from the International Association for Lichenology. Huge thanks to IAL for the honor!

entry.title: Lichen siderophore paper is out
entry.content:
A paper Gulnara contributed to is out in Nature Communications. The paper explores iron exchange as one of the aspects of lichen symbiosis, a first study of its sort. It shows that siderophore produced by the fungal symbiont in Xanthoria lichens enchances growth of the algal symbiont.

Was so great to be part of this study. Big thanks to Isidor Happacher and Hubertus Haas for putting this together!

entry.title: MetaLichenLab at EMBL symbiosis conference
entry.content: Gulnara presented her work on lichen secreted proteins at the EMBL Symposium “The cellular mechanics of symbiosis: sensing friend from foe” in Heidelberg, Germany. It was great to learn about great diversity of symbioses across the tree of life and different ways of studying them.
